body.text: Few places or corridors tell a richer story of geography and human movement than Khao soi. Stepping into its history reveals how trade, terrain, and culture shaped the modern map.

Khao soi or khao soy is a noodle dish from Northern Thailand made of wheat egg noodles in coconut milk curry, usually served with chicken or beef. Historically, it was also known as kway teow Ho. It is widely regarded as the most famous dish of Chiang Mai and of northern Thailand.
Its name is associated with the traditional method of cutting (soi) noodle dough into strips.

The dish is generally traced to Yunnanese Muslim traders, known in Thailand as Chin Ho, who travelled caravan routes into the Lanna region and settled in Chiang Mai in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, while Burmese and Indian cooking also influenced its development.

Khao soi is topped with deep-fried crispy noodles, and its curry paste combines dried chilies, shallots, garlic and spices such as black cardamom, coriander seeds and turmeric. Versions with pork and seafood have developed over time, and styles differ by region.

Related dishes include the Burmese ohn no khao swè, a Shan rice noodle dish called kao soi, and a very different Lao khao soi. The dish is usually served with pickled mustard greens, shallots, lime and roasted chili paste.

Khao soi is regarded as part of the multicultural culinary heritage of Lanna. Most of its energy comes from fat and carbohydrates, and researchers have developed higher-protein versions as well as ready-to-use curry paste and sauce products.
Although it is less known internationally than tom yum or pad thai, it has been promoted as part of Thai gastronomy tourism and soft power.
Etymology
Khao soi was once called kway teow Ho, a name that referred to its egg noodles served in curry broth. The name khao soi is linked to the way the noodles were made before machines were available.
Cooks mixed wheat flour, eggs, salt and water into a dough, rolled it into flat sheets and then cut (soi) the sheets into thin strips with a knife.

A similar explanation is given for the Shan dish kao soi: according to Jotika Khur-yearn of the Shan Cultural Association in London, kao means "rice" and soi means "to cut" in Shan, because the noodles were traditionally made by grinding, boiling and drying rice and then slicing it.
Writer Austin Bush has suggested another possibility. Several of the caravan routes passed through Myanmar, where the general word for noodles is the Shan term hkauk-hswe.
Bush suggests that this word was changed to khao soi in northern Thai and could have been used for almost any noodle dish, although he admits that this is speculation.
History
Khao soi developed within the multicultural food culture of Lanna, drawing on Chinese, Shan, Burmese and Indian influences that reached the region through trade and travel.

As Chiang Mai grew into a centre of trade, it attracted Shan, Burmese, Chinese and other traders, and dishes with foreign roots such as khao soi became established there before spreading across northern Thailand. The strongest influence is usually credited to Yunnanese Chinese Muslims, known in northern Thailand as Ho or Chin Ho.

Some popular accounts say that the dish evolved from Chin Haw Muslim traders who plied the spice route when the region was under Burmese control. The origin of the term Ho is uncertain, and it separates these overland migrants from the Chinese who came to Thailand by sea.
Caravan trade and settlement

Overland trade between Yunnan and Northern Thailand may date back to the 16th century. By the 19th century, caravans of Yunnanese traders, nearly all of them Hui Muslims from the Dali region of western Yunnan, travelled to northern Thailand every year during the cool, dry season, roughly from November to April.

Their main route ran from Simao in southern Yunnan through Kengtung in the Shan States, and some caravans continued through Chiang Mai to Mawlamyine (Moulmein) in Burma. According to Liulan Wang, the traders carried goods such as cotton textiles, silk, felt and medicines from Yunnan, and returned with ivory and traditional medicinal materials.

According to Eckhardt, these caravans travelled through the Shan State in Myanmar, Laos and Thailand from the 18th to the early 20th centuries. The caravan trade declined gradually in the early 20th century.

Some traders eventually settled in northern Thai cities, including Chiang Mai and Chiang Rai. In Chiang Mai, Yunnanese Muslim traders helped to found the Chang Phuak mosque in 1877, and in the early 20th century more Chin Ho settled east of the old walled city, in the area now known as Ban Ho.
In 1915, the ruler of Chiang Mai allowed the Chin Ho to settle and work in the city, and some of them opened shops selling khao soi made with freshly prepared noodles.
Khao soi begins to be mentioned around this period, as a dish said to have been sold and eaten only by Chin Ho, and it was originally halal.

Wang distinguishes these early Hui traders from a later and much larger wave of Yunnanese migration. After the Chinese Communists took power in 1949, soldiers of the defeated Nationalist Army (Kuomintang, KMT) and their supporters, most of whom were Han Chinese, fled from Yunnan through Burma into northern Thailand.

Before the 1950s, the Hui made up most of the Yunnanese in Thailand, but this migration made the Han the majority. By 1998, more than 80,000 Han Yunnanese and about 10,000 Hui Yunnanese lived in northern Thailand.

Many former KMT soldiers settled in the remote mountains of Chiang Mai, Chiang Rai and Mae Hong Son provinces, where they introduced tea growing and Yunnanese-Chinese dishes. Khao soi, however, is linked to the earlier Muslim community, which most likely introduced it to Chiang Mai.
Family histories collected by journalist Robyn Eckhardt show how the dish changed over time.

The Suthasinee restaurant was opened by the son of a Chin Ho trader who had sold a clear soup with rice noodles, and the son and his wife later replaced the rice noodles with egg noodles and added curry paste and coconut milk.

The owner of Khao Soi Lamduan Faham said that the shop's founder learned the dish from a Chin Ho cook who used hand-cut rice noodles coloured with turmeric, and that the founder changed to egg noodles and added curry paste to suit the northern Thai taste for spicy food.

There are several explanations for the coconut milk and spices. Coconut milk is rare in northern Thai cooking, which has led some writers to suggest that khao soi is a local version of the Burmese ohn no khao swè.
Chef Andy Ricker notes that, depending on the source, the dish's roots are credited to either Burmese or Chinese Muslim cooking, and he suggests that coconut milk may also have come from Burma.
Other vendors believe that coconut milk and dried spices were added to suit central Thai diners or Chiang Mai's Indian and Burmese communities.

A Chiang Mai University graduate student who researched khao soi suggested that Khao Soi Lamduan Faham added coconut milk to please its early customers, who were government officials from Bangkok, and that other shops then followed.

Other influences have also been described. Yaisumlee and colleagues note that Burmese people who worked in Lanna, many as foremen for British teak companies, brought dishes such as kaeng hang le and khanom chin nam ngiao, and also influenced khao soi.
Trade with Indian merchants introduced spices such as turmeric, curry powder and cumin, which give the curry its golden colour and depth of flavour.
Ingredients and preparation
The main components of khao soi are the noodles, a curry made from curry paste and coconut milk, meat, and seasonings such as fish sauce, soy sauce and sugar.
Noodles

Khao soi noodles are flat yellow wheat noodles made with chicken or duck eggs. Today they are usually rolled by machine, which gives them a soft but chewy texture. Each bowl contains the noodles in two forms: boiled noodles in the curry and a nest of deep-fried noodles on top, which adds a crunchy contrast.
